questions.q: What is an open redirection vulnerability?
o: A server that always 301-redirects every path to /home
A redirect whose destination comes from unvalidated input
A redirect that always leaks Referer to a third party
A CORS rule that allows every cross-origin Location header
questions.x: The app takes a user-controlled value and uses it as the redirect target, often in a Location header or in JavaScript, without checking that the destination is safe.
questions.h: Open means the destination is not locked down. What should be validated and is not?

questions.q: Where does a typical open redirect put the attacker-chosen URL?
o: In a Set-Cookie header that the browser must store
In a Location header or in a client-side redirect
In a Content-Security-Policy report-uri directive
In a Link preload header used for the next page fetch
questions.x: Common patterns are /redirect?url=, /login?return=, or /next?target=. The value is copied into a Location header or a client-side navigation with little or no allowlisting.
questions.h: HTTP redirects advertise the next URL in a specific response header. Client-side redirects set location instead.

questions.q: Consider these claims about open redirection. (1) It only works over HTTP, never HTTPS. (2) The destination is always hardcoded in the app. (3) It cannot be chained with other bugs. Which option is correct?
o: Only the first claim is true
Only the first two claims are true
Only the third claim is true
None of these statements are true
questions.x: Open redirects work on HTTPS just as well as HTTP. The destination comes from user input, not from a hardcoded safe path. They are used for phishing, filter bypass, and chains such as SSRF.
questions.h: Which of those three claims matches how an open redirect actually behaves?

questions.q: Why is open redirection useful for phishing even without SSRF?
o: It lets the attacker read session cookies from HttpOnly flags
The first URL is on a trusted host, then the user is sent off-site
It disables same-origin checks for the rest of the session
It puts the server private key into the redirect response body
questions.x: A link that starts on the real domain can still land on a fake login page. Users and some mail filters trust the first hostname and never inspect the redirect target.
questions.h: The click starts on a domain the victim already trusts. Where do they arrive after the redirect?

questions.q: Besides phishing, what else can an open redirect enable?
o: Direct remote code execution in the browser sandbox
Bypassing URL filters and chaining into bugs like SSRF
Forging TLS certificates for the victim's own domain
Reading files from the server disk without any request
questions.x: A legitimate host in the first URL can pass a filter that would block a raw internal address. If some other bug follows redirects, that open redirect becomes a stepping stone rather than a standalone phishing trick.
questions.h: Filters often allow the site's own host. What happens if that host then redirects somewhere the filter would have blocked?
